newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: COURT RULES AUSTRALIA PHONE COS MUST PAY COPYRIGHT.
newsitem.headline: COURT RULES AUSTRALIA PHONE COS MUST PAY COPYRIGHT.

text.p: The High Court ruled on Monday that Australia's largest telecommunications group, Telstra Corp, must pay copyright fees for all music played by "music on hold" systems over the telephone lines it rents out, Telstra said.
A Telstra spokesman said Telstra believed the decision meant all telephone companies would now have to pay copyright fees for any music played on hold by their customers.

An Australasian Performing Right Association (APRA) spokeswoman confirmed the court decision and said APRA would now hold discussions with the telephone companies over how the copyright fees would be paid.
"This judgement places the onus on Telstra to pay copyright royalties on behalf of its customers who use "Music on Hold" facilities," Telstra said.
"Telstra will therefore have to pay the copyright licence fees for which it is now liable, but does not expect the amount of these fees to be material."
Telstra spokesman Peter Hansen said it was too early to say how much the ruling might cost Telstra or the other telephone companies.
APRA spokeswoman Julie Harders told Reuters it was too early to say how much extra money would be raised by the ruling.
Telstra said the decision may also effect the transmission of copyright material other than on "music on hold". It said the internet and video conferencing may be affected.
The High Court ruling raised questions about the way copyright rights are based on the mechanism for delivering the transmission, rather than the actual source of the transmission, Telstra said.
"A technology neutral, broad based right to authorise transmissions to the public would certainly make the position of carriers more clear-cut," Telstra said.
Telstra welcomed the federal government's recent discussion paper which looked at the need for reform of the copyright laws.
The governmet-owned Telstra is due to be one-third privatised and floated in November. It's main competitor, the privately-held Optus Communications, is expected to float next year.
One of the other major telephone companies is Vodafone Australia Ltd, which is 95 percent owned by Vodafone Plc.
APRA chief executive Brett Cottle said the decision was very important for APRA's 20,000 members.
APRA manages the payment of royalties from radio and television stations to composers, songwriters and performers.
The court's three to two majority decision meant that Telstra and other carriers were liable for music broadcast on hold on land-based phone lines, Cottle said in a statement.
"Now APRA will be able to pay composers and songwriters royalties when their music is either transmitted over phone lines or broadcast to mobile phone receivers," Cottle said.
All five judges agreed Telstra infringed copyright by broadcasting music over mobile phone receivers, he said.
The High Court originally ruled two years ago that Telstra had infringed copyright by broadcasting music over its phone lines.
Telstra appealed last year and Thursday's decision was a ruling on that appeal.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
